catalog_quote: 1.3 Stress Placement. Word stress is phonemic only by virtue of a small class of stems in which stress is unpredictable. In the majority of words, however, stress occurs on the penult or, in the case of words with the paragoge -ɨq, on the antepenult, unless the vowel in those syllables is the high central ɨ. Where ɨ does occur, stress placement moves in the progressive direction except in words where there is no vowel but ɨ, in which case, again, the placement of stress is quite unpredictable. For other words, [p. 269] although recourse to the grammar would reveal regular stress movement rules, stress placement purely in terms of the phonology itself is often arbitrary.[4] 'lebang 'pry', le'bang 'licked at'; 'kapang 'fishtrap', ka'pang 'group (of animals, etc.)'; 'kapu 'rub', ka'pu 'desire, want' [...] [p. 272] 2.3 Stress. Stress and high pitch in Sangiré words are observed to be allophones of the same phoneme. The treatment here is limited to primary word stress due to the need for further study of secondary stress. ['(C)V] Stress. Occurs on any one syllable back to the antepenult, normally excepting those syllables with ɨ but occurring on any of them but the paragoge when they contain no vowel other than ɨ (e.g. ka'pantagɨq 'use, purpose', 'batu 'stone', tɨ'aq 'fly', ma'kɨgɨng 'dried', malɨ'gɨng 'sad').

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress (realised as stress plus high pitch) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the paragogic syllable -ɨq does not count, so words ending in it are stressed on the antepenult (i.e. the penult of the base). A syllable whose vowel is the high central ɨ (schwa-like) is skipped and stress moves one syllable to the right (e.g. tɨ'aq 'fly', malɨ'ging 'sad'); if every vowel is ɨ the position is unpredictable (Scheller 1991 p. 7 finds only penult in such words). Stress can thus stand on the antepenult, penult or final syllable, but the penult is the default; Sneddon 1984 p. 21 restates the same rule with 'except if [the penult] contains ə and the final syllable contains some other vowel, in which case stress falls on the final syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Maryott 1977 p. 272 explicitly defers secondary stress ('need for further study'). Scheller 1991 sec. 2.2 p. 7: in words of more than three syllables secondary stress is observed on the third or fourth syllable preceding the primary-stressed one (e.g. /ˌka.la.laŋ.'sun/, /qi.ˌpɨ.pɨ.bi.'sa.la/), but 'stress is not predictable'.
new_statements.exceptions: A 'small class of stems' with unpredictable, contrastive stress: 'lebang 'pry' vs le'bang 'licked at', 'kapang 'fishtrap' vs ka'pang 'group', 'kapu 'rub' vs ka'pu 'desire' (p. 269); fn. 4 (pp. 277-278) derives these from the suffix allomorph -ng (< -ang, stress advancing one syllable), a fossilised root-final -ng, and vowel coalescence after loss of a lateral (Sangihé ka'pulu). Scheller 1991 adds that possessive suffixes on vowel-final nouns move stress rightward (/'ba.le/ > /ba.'le.nu/) while consonant-final nouns keep it (/'qa.baq/ > /'qa.baq.u/; sec. 2.1 p. 6, sec. 4.1 p. 15), and that stress is never on a final syllable containing the paragoge /-ɨq/. Sneddon 1984 p. 53 gives the historical source: Proto-Sangiric penult stress shifted off penultimate schwa in Sangil.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms, phonemic (typewritten) transcription; stress and high pitch are treated as allophones of one suprasegmental phoneme, and fn. 8 (p. 278) notes that phrase intonation (emphasised phrase-final enclitics) can neutralise the raised pitch of the stressed syllable and lengthen it in expressive speech. The original prints the high central vowel as barred i (transcribed ɨ here) and the glottal stop as q. Data are the Sarangani Islands dialect (Maryott notes a distinct Mindanao dialect, p. 278 fn. 5).
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary descriptions (Maryott 1977, Scheller 1991, Sneddon 1984 sec. 2.1.2) describe the Sarangani Islands dialect of Sangil, which Maryott and SIL call 'Sarangani Sangiré' (endonym [saŋiraʔ]); Sneddon 1984 p. 6 explicitly equates Maryott's 'Sangiré' with the language called Sangil in the literature (his 'Snl'), and Glottolog files all three works under sang1337 / ISO snl. Maryott (p. 278 fn. 5) notes a separate Mindanao-mainland dialect that lacks the retroflex lateral phoneme; no separate glottocode. Not to be confused with Sangir/Sangihé of Indonesia (sxn, sang1336), whose phonology Maryott 1961 describes and which Sneddon treats separately (stress fully predictable on the penult there, p. 20).

Regular stress falls on the penult, except if this contains ə and the final syllable contains some other vowel, in which case stress falls on the final syllable, e.g. bátu stone, kagə́ dried but taá? fly, kə́kkə́? fist.
